I hear your frustration, and I want to be honest: there is no simple, intellectual answer that can take away the pain or the outrage when children suffer. For many, these aren't just theological questions—they are deeply emotional wounds.

Based on Christian perspectives, here are a few ways this difficult reality is understood:

*   **Human Freedom and Choice:** One perspective is that God gives human beings genuine freedom. This means people are free to choose how they act, and unfortunately, some choose to corrupt what is good and commit horrific acts of abuse or violence. From this view, the suffering caused by these actions is not God's fault, but a result of human choices (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)).
*   **A Broken World:** Some explain that suffering happens because we live in a world where sin and brokenness are present. This includes not only the intentional evil of people but also "natural" suffering like disease and accidents, which occur because the world does not function as God originally intended (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this](https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this)).
*   **God's Presence in Suffering:** Rather than offering a reason *why* every specific tragedy happens, some point to the person of Jesus. The belief is that God did not remain distant from our pain; instead, He entered into human suffering Himself. By experiencing extreme suffering on the cross, Jesus showed that God is not indifferent to our pain but is "suffering with" us (thelife, [https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3](https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3)).
*   **The Promise of Justice:** There is also the belief that while justice is not always served in this life, God assures that everyone will eventually answer for their actions and that ultimate justice will be administered (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)).

I realize these answers may still feel incomplete or insufficient when faced with the reality of a child's pain. If you're open to it, I'm here to listen more or explore any of these points further with you.

It is completely understandable that this feels like a contradiction; many people find it to be one of the most mysterious and confounding parts of the Christian faith (Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?").

When Christians speak about the Trinity, they are trying to describe a reality that they believe is revealed in the Bible: that there is only one God, but He exists eternally as three distinct Persons—the Father, the Son (Jesus), and the Holy Spirit (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief").

To help make sense of this, theologians often distinguish between **essence** and **person**:

*   **Essence (What God is):** "Essence" refers to the "being" or "nature" of God. Christians believe there is only one divine essence. Because there is only one essence, there is only one God (Cru, "Entender la Trinidad").
*   **Person (Who God is):** While there is one essence, there are three distinct Persons. This means the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not just different "roles" or "masks" God wears, but distinct individuals who have loved and interacted with one another for all eternity (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief"; Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?").

**Why it's not seen as a contradiction:**
From this perspective, it would only be a contradiction if Christians claimed God was three in the *same way* He is one. Instead, they believe He is one in essence and three in person (Cru, "Entender la Trinidad"). One source suggests thinking of it not as addition (1+1+1=3), but more like multiplication (1x1x1=1) (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?").

**Common Illustrations:**
Because this is so difficult to grasp, people often use analogies, though most admit these are imperfect:
*   **Water:** H2O can exist as ice, liquid water, or steam. They look and behave differently, but the essence (H2O) is the same (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?"; EveryStudent — German, "Dreieinigkeit").
*   **The Sun:** One sun provides light, heat, and radiation—three distinct aspects coming from one source (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?").

Ultimately, many Christians acknowledge that because God is spirit and exists beyond the limitations of our three-dimensional universe, the Trinity is something that cannot be fully grasped by human logic alone (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?").

It is completely understandable why that sounds like a contradiction. It is one of the most mysterious and confounding doctrines in the Christian faith, and many people find it difficult to grasp because it doesn't fit into our everyday human experience (Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?").

To help make sense of it, theologians often distinguish between two different words: **essence** and **person**.

### Essence vs. Person
The core idea is that God is **one in essence** but **three in person**.

*   **Essence (What God is):** Essence refers to God's "being" or "substance." Think of this as the "what." Christians believe there is only one divine essence or one single "being" that is God (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief"; Cru, "Entender la Trinidad").
*   **Person (Who God is):** "Person" refers to the distinct identities within that one essence. The three Persons are the Father, the Son (Jesus), and the Holy Spirit (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief").

A way to look at it mathematically is that it isn't $1 + 1 + 1 = 3$, but rather $1 \times 1 \times 1 = 1$ (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?").

### Why it isn't considered a contradiction
According to the source *Cru*, a contradiction would only exist if someone said God is three in the *same way* He is one. However, because He is one in *essence* (what He is) and three in *person* (who He is), the two truths can coexist (Cru, "Entender la Trinidad").

The Bible presents these distinctions through the relationships between the three:
*   The Father sends the Son (John 3:16).
*   The Father and Son send the Holy Spirit (John 14:26; Acts 2:33).
*   Because they interact with one another, they must be distinct Persons, yet they all share the same divine nature (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief").

### Common Illustrations
Because this is so hard to visualize, people often use analogies, though most sources note that no human illustration is perfect (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?"):
*   **Water (H2O):** It can exist as liquid, ice, or steam. It looks and acts differently, but the essence is always H2O (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?"; EveryStudent German, "Dreieinigkeit").
*   **The Sun:** From the sun, we receive light, heat, and radiation. These are three distinct aspects, but they all come from the one sun (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?").

Ultimately, while these tools can help explain the concept, many Christians view the Trinity as a profound mystery that exceeds human understanding (Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?").

That is a very fair and direct question. To be honest and clear: the Gospels do not record Jesus ever saying the exact phrase, "I am God" (Sightline Ministry, [Two Reasons Skeptics Believe Jesus is not God](https://sightlinemiristry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god)).

However, there are several instances where Jesus used words and titles that his listeners understood as claims to be God. Here are a few examples of his exact words from the text:

*   **"The Father and I are one"** (John 10:30). According to Sightline Ministry ([Did Jesus Say He Is God?](https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god)), the Greek word for "one" in this context suggests being one in essence or nature.
*   **"Before Abraham was born, I am!"** (John 8:58). The Jesus Film Project ([40 Interesting Facts about Jesus](https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts)) notes that "I AM" is the specific name God used when speaking to Moses from the burning bush.
*   **"Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father"** (John 14:9), as cited by Sightline Ministry ([Two Reasons Skeptics Believe Jesus is not God](https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god)).

The reactions of the people around him often provide a clue to how they interpreted his words. For example, after Jesus said he was one with the Father in John 10:30-33, the devout Jews attempted to execute him for blasphemy, stating, "You, a mere man, claim to be God" (Cru, [Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?](https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html)).

I hear your question, and I want to be very honest with you: if you are looking for the specific, literal phrase, **"I am God,"** you won't find that exact sentence in the Gospels (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god](https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god)).

However, the New Testament records several instances where Jesus makes claims that his listeners understood as a claim to divinity. Here are the specific words recorded in the text:

*   **"Before Abraham was, I am!"** (John 8:58). According to the Jesus Film Project, this is significant because Jesus used the same name ("I am") that God used when speaking to Moses from the burning bush in Exodus 3:14 (Jesus Film Project, [https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts](https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts)).
*   **"I am."** When the high priest asked him directly, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed [God]?", Jesus replied, "I am" (Cru, [https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html](https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html)).
*   **"The Father and I are one"** (John 10:30). Sightline Ministry notes that some scholars believe the Greek word for "one" here refers to being one in essence or nature (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god](https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god)).
*   **"Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father"** (John 14:9) (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god](https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god)).

The accounts suggest that the people listening to him—specifically the religious leaders of the time—understood these statements as a claim to be God. For example, in John 5:18, it is noted that the Jewish leaders tried to kill him because they believed he was "making himself equal with God" (Jesus Film Project, [https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts](https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts)).

I know that "interpreting" statements can feel different from hearing a direct declaration, and I appreciate you asking for the distinction. Does seeing these specific passages help clarify what you were looking for, or does it raise more questions?

It's very common to hear that concern, and it's a fair question to ask when you think about how long ago the Bible was written. While it's true that the Bible has been copied and translated many times, scholars argue that we can still know what was originally written with a high degree of accuracy.

Here are a few points that might help you think through this:

*   **The Number of Copies:** We have a massive number of ancient handwritten copies (manuscripts). For example, there are nearly 25,000 handwritten copies of portions of the New Testament (EveryStudent, "Jesus in Islam"). Having so many copies allows scholars to compare and cross-check them to reconstruct the original text (Sightline Ministry, "Has the Bible Been Altered Over the Centuries?").
*   **Consistency Across Copies:** When historians compare these manuscripts, they've found that the New Testament we have today is at least 99.5% accurate to the original (EveryStudent, "Jesus in Islam"). Most of the 0.5% difference involves things like spelling or word order, which do not change the actual meaning (EveryStudent — Vietnamese, "Các sách của Kinh Thánh - Lịch sử của Kinh Thánh").
*   **Direct Translation:** A common misconception is that the Bible was translated from one language to another, and then that translation was translated again, like a game of "telephone." However, modern translations are actually made directly from the original Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic based on those thousands of ancient manuscripts (EveryStudent — Vietnamese, "Các sách của Kinh Thánh - Lịch sử của Kinh Thánh").
*   **Archaeological Evidence:** Findings like the Dead Sea Scrolls have shown that the Bible we have today remains highly similar, and nearly 100% identical, to texts from a very long time ago (EveryStudent, "Jesus in Islam").

In short, while human scribes did occasionally make small mistakes, the sheer volume of available manuscripts allows scholars to identify those errors and maintain the integrity of the original message (Sightline Ministry, "The Bible: How Big a Deal is Human Error?").

It is very understandable why your uncle might feel that way. When we think about things being copied by hand for thousands of years, it’s natural to worry that the message might have gotten lost or changed along the way.

However, many scholars and historians point to evidence that suggests the Bible has been preserved with a very high degree of accuracy. Here are a few points that might help you navigate that conversation:

*   **The sheer number of copies:** We don't have the very first pieces of paper the authors wrote on, but we have thousands of ancient handwritten copies (called manuscripts). For example, there are over 24,000 handwritten copies of portions of the New Testament (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)).
*   **Cross-checking for accuracy:** Because there are so many different copies from different places and times, scholars can compare them against one another. This allows them to "cross-check" the texts to see where differences occur. This process helps researchers reconstruct what the original writings most likely said with a very high degree of accuracy (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries](https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries)).
*   **High percentage of agreement:** Historians have noted that when comparing these manuscripts, the New Testament is estimated to be at least 99.5% accurate to the original (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)). The small differences that do exist are often just minor things like spelling or word order, which don't change the actual meaning of the text (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)).
*   **Ancient discoveries:** Finds like the Dead Sea Scrolls have also shown that the biblical texts remained incredibly similar to the versions we use today (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)).

So, while it's true that human error exists in any hand-copied document, the massive amount of evidence available allows us to identify those errors and see that the core message has been faithfully passed down (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error](https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error)).
